finding.doh_comparison.blocked: The name is refused or blocked by {providers} while other resolvers resolve it: security filtering (domain judged malicious) or censorship.
finding.doh_comparison.sinkhole: {providers} returns a non-public address (sinkhole, poisoning or split-horizon) while the other resolvers return a public one.
module.doh_comparison.checks: Resolves the target through Cloudflare and Google (DNS over HTTPS, RFC 8484), Quad9 (DNS over TLS) and the local resolver, then compares: filtering or censorship, non-public addresses, DNSSEC validation.
module.doh_comparison.fix:
Compare the answers of several resolvers for your name (commands in the snippet): if only one differs, note which one (Cloudflare, Google, Quad9 or your local resolver) and the value it returns. Different addresses behind a CDN are normal.
Name refused or blocked by a public resolver: first check that your site is not compromised (phishing, malware, injected pages), the most common cause of a security block; clean up, update and change passwords if needed.
Once the site is clean, ask for the unblock from the provider of the filtering resolver, through its dispute or false-positive report form; allow some time.
Non-public address returned by a single resolver: if it is your local resolver, check the router, the firewall and the machines' `hosts` file, and change the DNS of the workstation or router if it is hijacked; if it is an intended split-horizon, document it.
Check that all your name servers publish the same zone by comparing their SOA serial number (`dig +short SOA example.com @ns1.example.net`): an out-of-sync zone gives different answers from one resolver to another.
To protect your users against forged answers, enable DNSSEC on the domain (DNSSEC module) and use a validating, encrypting resolver (DoT or DoH) on workstations.
Run the scan again to confirm that all resolvers return the same answer.
module.doh_comparison.fix_snippet:
# Bash
dig +short example.com @1.1.1.1
dig +short example.com @8.8.8.8
dig +short example.com @9.9.9.9
dig +short example.com

# PowerShell
Resolve-DnsName example.com -Type A -Server 1.1.1.1
Resolve-DnsName example.com -Type A -Server 8.8.8.8
Resolve-DnsName example.com -Type A -Server 9.9.9.9
Resolve-DnsName example.com -Type A
module.doh_comparison.title: Encrypted DNS comparison (DoH/DoT)
module.doh_comparison.why: A resolver refusing a name that the others resolve signals blocking (security filtering, censorship); an internal address returned by only one betrays poisoning or split-horizon.
